newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stands firm on N.Korea nuclear waste deal.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stands firm on N.Korea nuclear waste deal.

text.p: Taiwan Vice-President Lien Chan said on Saturday his government would not intervene in a plan to ship nuclear waste to North Korea, saying it was a lawful, safe business deal with no moral issue involved.

"As long as the deal complies with international regulations and the shipment is legal and safe, the government will not intervene," Lien Chan, who is also premier, told reporters at a Lunar New Year news conference.
Lien was referring to a controversial January 11 pact, signed by state-run Taiwan Power Co and a North Korean agency, to ship up to 200,000 barrels of nuclear waste to Pyongyang.
Lien said Taiwan's Republic of China was not the first government to dispose its nuclear waste overseas.
"According to my understanding and looking at future development, (overseas disposal) of low-radioactive nuclear material is becoming more important and pervasive," Lien said.
"The Republic of China (Taiwan) is definitely not the first."
The Taipei-Pyongyang nuclear waste deal triggered militant protests in South Korea, which has expressed concerns about nuclear contamination on the Korean peninsula.
On Thursday, seven South Korean activists were deported by Taipei after clashing with supporters of the shipments outside Taiwan Power's headquarters.
The seven were deported for breaching Taiwan's assembly law, a police official said.
North and South Korea remain technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended with a truce, not a peace treaty.
International environmentalist group Greenpeace condemned the plan, accusing cash-rich but diplomatically isolated Taiwan of "blatantly exploiting North Korea".
Lien said the waste agreement was one of mutual consent.
"This is the kind of business activity that conforms to international laws. No one side is forcing the other; no one side is using illegal means to cheat the other," Lien said.
"There is no moral issue in this case."
Another South Korean anti-nuclear delegation, which includes four South Korean parliament deputies, arrived in Taiwan on Friday to pressure the government to cancel the deal.
They gave a protest petition signed by 156 Korean lawmakers to Taiwan deputy parliament speaker Wang Jin-pyng, pledging to "expend utmost effort to try to revoke the contract".

"We will also negotiate with neighbouring countries to prevent North Korea from becoming a nuclear waste dump," the petition said. "We sincerely urge Taiwan's government to consider the request by South Korea parliament members and cancel the plan to ship nuclear waste to North Korea."
The group met Taipower officials but reached no conclusion.
Taipei has reiterated its determination to press ahead with the waste shipments, despite growing pressure from South Korea and communist China -- Taiwan's arch rival.
China on Thursday criticised the deal as a blatant bid by Taipei to spoil Beijing's ties with its Stalinist neighbour.

China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has toned down what had been intimate ties with North Korea since establishing formal relations in 1992 with South Korea, Pyongyang's sworn enemy.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with either North or South Korea, both of which recognise Beijing.
The United States has said any waste shipment to North Korea from Taiwan should conform to international standards.
